To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

GnRH is present in the retina of all species examined, but is more concentrated in the butterflyfish and damselfish than the wrasse and goby; GnRH receptors are present in the retina and diencephalic and tectal visual centers of all species examined; GnRH is present at multiple levels of the visual system, from retina to optic tectum, in all species; GnRH receptors were found in the tectum and diencephalon of all species examined.

GnRH-ir terminals are present in the retina and visual centers in four species of coral reef fishes, and that GnRH receptors colocalize with GnRH-IR axons in the retina and with GnRH- ir terminals in visual centers.

GnRH and GnRH receptor distribution patterns are conserved across four coral reef fish species at multiple levels in the visual processing pathway, but that species-specific variations exist in GnRH innervations of the retina, suggesting possible species-specific functions of GnRH in visual processing.
